results.content: # How to address EHR alert fatigue. EHR alert fatigue overwhelming clinician. EHR alert fatigue overwhelming clinician. Electronic health record (EHR) systems feature pop-up alerts to deliver critical patient data to clinicians in real-time. This guide addresses EHR alert fatigue and offers practical solutions to optimize alert effectiveness. Fortunately, informing yourself and your staff and addressing alert fatigue can lower the risk of adverse patient events, support better care delivery, and relieve clinician burnout to enhance professional quality of life. ### Causes of EHR alert fatigue. This metric centers on clinician experience when evaluating how alert fatigue affects your practice. ## Strategies to mitigate EHR alert fatigue. EHR systems that allow practices and health systems to configure alert delivery help reduce the risk of alert fatigue for clinical and non-clinical staff. Effective strategies for mitigating alert fatigue focus on customization, clinician engagement, and interventions informed by data-driven insights using tailored solutions designed to meet the practice’s specific needs.

results.content: # Best Practices to Mitigate EHR Clinical Decision Alert Fatigue. ## Healthcare organizations across the country are finding creative ways to reduce EHR clinical decision alert fatigue through optimization and teamwork. EHR alerts serve a significant purpose, but they can also result in EHR clinical decision alert fatigue, clinician burnout, or even frustration. EHR alerts permit clinicians to access real-time patient data, ideally resulting in enhanced patient safety and medication accuracy. According to Stanford University health IT professionals, EHR alerts are a vital part of EHRs that are “not merely the use of technology; it is using technology to find meaningful information to make clinical decisions and provide the best possible patient care.”. Clinician burnout and EHR fatigue caused by alerts have been an issue for clinicians struggling with EHR usability overload. Although EHR alerts can offer providers practical suggestions and updates, EHR alert fatigue has been an issue for clinicians already struggling with EHR usability problems. Low-value EHR alerts can disrupt patient care and contribute to clinician burnout. “The way myself and other leaders in the alert space think about it is, EHR alerts should fire when the clinician needs to be shown something,” Bates said. A similar practice occurred at Vanderbilt University Medical Center (VUMC), when Vanderbilt Clinical Informatics Center (VCLIC) launched the Clickbusters program to minimize the number of EHR alerts. Communication between a health organization and its clinicians is vital to minimize EHR alert fatigue. According to a study published in the *Yearbook of Medical Informatics*, gathering clinician feedback and engineering communication between the healthcare organization and clinicians can improve both EHR alert fatigue and mitigate clinician burnout. Following implementation, EHR alert efficiency and effectiveness should be measured to see its impact on workflow, override rates, clinician burnout, and patient outcomes. As is with EHRs and other forms of health IT, EHR alerts require ongoing optimization and updates to adhere to current medical standards. At Rush University Medical Center, a hospital-wide survey led leaders to implement a team of health IT and EHR professionals to work one-on-one with its clinicians, called the Provider Optimization and Experience Team (POET). EHR alerts aim to be helpful, but alerts can also lead to severe clinician burnout and fatigue.

results.title: Reducing Alert Fatigue in EHRs: An AI-Driven Dashboard Prototype
results.content: # Reducing Alert Fatigue in EHRs: An AI-Driven Dashboard Prototype. Alert fatigue is one of the most overlooked risks in modern healthcare. To explore how this might be addressed, I built a lightweight, proof-of-concept dashboard using synthetic clinical alert data, simulated AI dismissal risk scoring, and Power BI Web. While this isn’t a production tool or trained ML model, the goal was to prototype how thoughtful visualization and predictive thinking could reduce cognitive burden and support better decision-making. * “Which alerts are being dismissed most often?”. * “Are critical alerts being ignored?”. * “What kinds of alerts are most likely to be ignored?”. * “Can we predict which alerts are likely to be overridden?”. * Suppress alerts that are frequently dismissed and low risk. * Adjust logic for high-risk alerts with high override rates. * Tailor alerts based on department (ICU vs outpatient vs ED). * Key Metrics: Total alerts, dismissal %, high severity %. * AI Scoring: A simulated “Dismissal Likelihood Score” per alert. * Trend Visuals: Alert volume over time. * Slicers for Interactivity: Severity, alert type, dismissal status. * Synthetic EHR Data: 100 mock alerts with simulated attribute. * In a production version, each department could load only relevant alerts based on clinician role. * Some “high severity” alerts were dismissed just as often as low ones. * Certain alert types had >80% dismissal rate, suggesting they may no longer be useful. Dr Terence Tan 1 year ago. * It encourages clinicians and informatics teams to think about alert usefulness, not just alert frequency. * How do we measure "alert fatigue" quantitatively? * Researchers studying alert fatigue, CDS (Clinical Decision Support), and EHR UX. * Clinical systems analysts looking to improve EHR alert logic and human-system interaction. How Clinical Context Changes Things Not all alerts are created equal. * Filtering alerts by diagnosis severity (e.g., sepsis vs chronic conditions). With alert fatigue continuing to be one of the challenges in clinical setting, this is a great starting point for anyone exploring how AI and visualization can improve clinical decision support. * ### AI in Healthcare: Risk or Reward? Title: How Brigham and Women’s Hospital is Relieving EHR Alert Fatigue | TechTarget
## EHR alert fatigue has been running rampant throughout hospitals, but health IT leaders at Brigham and Women’s Hospital might have found a solution. “An EHR alert appears and clinicians develop a reflex to immediately close it,” David Bates, MD, chief of the Division of General Internal Medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, said in an interview with *EHRIntelligence*. Bates and his team of researchers found that Brigham and Women’s clinicians were getting roughly one alert for every two medication orders, and clinicians were overriding approximately 98 percent of the alerts. Although warnings can offer providers practical suggestions and updates, EHR alert fatigue has been an issue for clinicians already struggling with EHR usability problems. Low-value EHR alerts can disrupt patient care and contribute to clinician burnout. “One of the big issues is that many of the clinical systems that are in routine use today, alert too frequently,” said Bates, who also doubles as a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. Unsatisfied with how their EHR vendor fired off alerts, Bates and his health IT team tapped Seegnal eHealth to leverage its EHR alert solution and conduct an EHR alert study at the Boston-based hospital. “We looked at how often the alerts were valid and we also looked at how the clinicians responded to them,” Bates explained. “The biggest finding was that moving to this approach would eliminate 93 percent of the medication-related alerts that clinicians see now, which would be a big change.”. It also presented the alert in a way that the clinician could immediately tell how crucial the alert is and what the next step should be in the clinical process. “It doesn't tell the clinician which antidepressant to prescribe, but it does tell the user of the available ones, which ones are not going to cause a problem given the medications that the patient's already on.”. Following the study results, Bates said he is excited to fully integrate the alert solution into the EHR system, anticipating approval from the Brigham in the near future. “The way myself and other leaders in the alert space think about it is, EHR alerts should fire when the clinician needs to be shown something,” Bates said.
